Friday. "Can I go to the fair with Meenal?" Gopika asked. "No." "Why?" "Because I said so," said her mother, Sangeeta, still chopping onions. Gopika's face flushed. "You never trust me!" Sangeeta put the knife down hard. "Don't talk to me in that tone."
Sunday. Gopika asked to walk to the library alone. "No, and don't argue." "You treat me like a criminal!" Sangeeta turned away, jaw tight. Under the words, she kept seeing the news story about the girl near the station, but she didn't say it.
Wednesday. Gopika didn't ask anything. She put her earphones in at dinner. Sangeeta ate in silence. Both felt disrespected. Neither had said the real thing yet.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta chopping when Gopika asked about the fair?
qa.a: She was chopping onions.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling underneath her "because I said so"?
qa.a: She was worried for Gopika's safety, thinking of the news story about the girl near the station, but she did not say it.

qa.q: What turning point is available to both of them at this stage?
qa.a: Sangeeta could say she is scared rather than just no, and Gopika could say she wants to be trusted rather than attacking, so the real feelings come out.

qa.q: How does Gopika hear "because I said so"?
qa.a: She hears it as disrespect and a sign that her mother doesn't trust her at all, so she protests and then shuts down.

grounding: It shows a parent's flat command and a teen's protest, each hearing disrespect while worry and the wish to be trusted stay unsaid.

passage:
Afreen, you think your Abba is too strict? Let your neighbour Jagdish Dada tell you about my son Manoj, when he was sixteen. He wanted to go on a bike trip with his friends to the hills. I said no. He asked why. I said, "Because I am your father, and I said so." He shouted, "You never trust me! You think I'm still a child!" I felt he was insulting me. He felt I was insulting him. We didn't speak for two days. Only years later did he tell me he just wanted me to see he had grown up. And I never told him that I had lost a school friend on that same road.
We both said the wrong words, beta.

qa.q: Where did Manoj want to go with his friends?
qa.a: He wanted to go on a bike trip to the hills.

qa.q: What was Jagdish Dada really afraid of when he said no?
qa.a: He was afraid because he had lost a school friend on that same road, but he never said it to Manoj.

qa.q: What could Jagdish Dada and Manoj have said instead?
qa.a: Jagdish Dada could have shared his fear about the road, and Manoj could have said he wanted to be seen as grown up, which might have started a real talk.

qa.q: How did Manoj experience his father's answer?
qa.a: He felt his father saw him as a child and didn't trust him, which is why he shouted.

grounding: It illustrates a parent saying because I said so and a teen replying you never trust me, both hearing disrespect while hiding worry and the wish to be trusted.

The school trip to Rishikesh left at five in the morning, and the form had to be signed by that evening. Jasleen waited until her mother, Kalyani, got home from her hospital shift, exhausted, still in her uniform.

"Mumma, sign this? Everyone's going."

Kalyani glanced at it. "River rafting? No."

"Why?"

"Because I said so."

Jasleen's face went hot. "You never trust me. Ever. You think I'm going to drown in a river with forty teachers watching?"

"Don't take that tone with me."

"You don't even listen!"

Kalyani set her bag down hard. Under the tiredness was a picture of brown water and a capsized raft she'd seen on the news. She didn't say it.

Jasleen didn't say that what she really wanted was for her mother to believe she could handle something. They both just heard disrespect.

qa.q: What activity was on the trip form?
qa.a: River rafting.

qa.q: What was Jasleen really wanting underneath "You never trust me"?
qa.a: She was hungry to be trusted, to have her mother believe she could handle something, and she felt hurt and angry.

qa.q: What went wrong in this exchange, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Each spoke in commands and accusations; if Kalyani said she was scared of the river and Jasleen said she wanted to be trusted, they could talk about safety plans.

qa.q: What is Kalyani feeling as she sets her bag down hard?
qa.a: She is exhausted, worried about the river, and stung by what she hears as disrespect.

grounding: Kalyani says "because I said so" and Jasleen answers "you never trust me"; each hears disrespect while hiding worry and a wish to be trusted.

passage:
Aparna came in at 9:40, forty minutes past curfew, and her father, Nitin, was waiting in the hall of their Indore flat.

"Where were you?"

"At Riddhi's. I told you. We were finishing the project."

"You were supposed to be home by nine. From now on, straight home after school. That's final."

"What? Why?"

"Because I said so."

"You never trust me! It was forty minutes!"

"Don't raise your voice at me."

"You raised yours first!"

Aparna slammed her bag down. Nitin felt his chest tighten: for forty minutes he had been calling her phone and imagining things he didn't want to imagine. But all he could say was, "Go to your room."

Aparna went, thinking: he doesn't care what I did, only that I obeyed. Neither of them said the thing that was true.

qa.q: How late past curfew was Aparna?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling during those forty minutes?
qa.a: He was frightened and anxious, calling her phone and imagining terrible things.

qa.q: What could each say instead of "Because I said so" and "You never trust me"?
qa.a: Nitin could say he was scared when she didn't answer; Aparna could say she wants to be trusted and should have called.

qa.q: How does Aparna read her father's anger?
qa.a: She reads it as caring only about obedience, not about her, and feels hurt and mistrusted.

grounding: Nitin commands and Aparna protests, each hearing disrespect, while his worry and her wish to be trusted stay unspoken.

"Bhavna, no phone at the dinner table."

"I'm just replying to Ishita, Mumma."

"Now. Give it."

"Why?"

"Because I said so."

"You never trust me! I'm not doing anything wrong."

"I didn't say you were."

"Then why are you taking it?"

"Because I said so, Bhavna."

"You always say that. You never explain anything."

"Don't talk to me like that in front of your brother."

"Like what? I'm just asking!"

Sarika held out her hand. Bhavna put the phone in it, hard.

What Sarika didn't say: she'd read about kids being bullied online, and Bhavna had been quiet all week. What Bhavna didn't say: Ishita was upset about her parents, and she was trying to help. Both just heard disrespect.

qa.q: Who was Bhavna replying to?
qa.a: Ishita.

qa.q: What was Sarika worried about but didn't say?
qa.a: She was anxious that Bhavna might be bullied online, because Bhavna had been quiet all week.

qa.q: What could turn this around?
qa.a: Sarika could explain her worry and Bhavna could say she was helping Ishita, so they talk about the real feelings instead of the command.

qa.q: How does Bhavna experience "Because I said so"?
qa.a: She feels mistrusted and dismissed, since she was only trying to help a friend.

grounding: In a dinner-table exchange Sarika says "because I said so" and Bhavna says "you never trust me", each hearing disrespect and hiding the real feeling.

It was about the school trip to Munnar. Ujjwal's class was going, mine too: three days, two nights. Achan read the permission slip at the dining table and put it down. "No."
"Why?"
"Because I said so."
I remember the heat climbing up my neck. "You never trust me. Never!"
He stood up, chair scraping. "Don't raise your voice at me, Gopika."
I went to my room and slammed the door, and through it I heard him tell Amma, "She has no respect." I lay there thinking exactly the same about him. Looking back, neither of us said the real thing. I didn't say, "I want you to see I can look after myself." He didn't say whatever he was afraid of. We both heard only disrespect, and we fought that instead.

qa.q: What trip did Gopika want permission for?
qa.a: The school trip to Munnar: three days, two nights.

qa.q: What did Gopika really want Achan to understand?
qa.a: She wanted Achan to see she could look after herself; under her angry words was a hurt, hungry wish to be trusted.

qa.q: What could either of them have said instead to change this stage?
qa.a: Achan could have named his worry about the trip, and Gopika could have asked what he was afraid of, instead of trading commands and accusations.

qa.q: How might Achan have heard 'You never trust me'?
qa.a: He likely heard it as rudeness and disrespect, which made him defend his authority instead of sharing the worry underneath.

grounding: Shows a parent's 'because I said so' meeting a teen's 'you never trust me', with each hearing disrespect and the real feelings left unsaid.
